lesson.title: No Promises, Just an Attempt
lesson.summary: Best effort delivery is the guarantee, or lack of one, that underlies connectionless protocols: the network will try to deliver each datagram but will not detect or repair loss, duplication, or reordering, a deliberate simplicity that keeps routers fast and pushes reliability decisions up to whoever actually needs them.
lesson.body:
Best effort delivery describes exactly what a connectionless protocol promises once it hands a datagram to the network: an honest attempt to deliver it, and nothing more. There is no acknowledgment confirming the datagram arrived, no automatic retransmission if it is lost, no correction if it arrives after a later datagram sent afterward, and no detection if a duplicate copy shows up. If something goes wrong anywhere along the path, from the sender's own network interface to a congested router in the middle to a receiver that is too busy to accept the data, the datagram is simply gone, and neither the network nor the connectionless protocol itself does anything about it.

IP, the network layer protocol underlying the entire internet, is the canonical best effort service. When a router's outgoing queue for a link is full, the standard behavior is simply to drop the incoming packet rather than somehow guarantee its delivery, and no notification is sent back to the original sender by the network layer itself. UDP, sitting directly on top of IP at the transport layer, inherits this same best effort character, since it adds port based addressing but does not add any of the sequencing or retransmission machinery that would be needed to detect or repair a drop.

It is tempting to read best effort as simply a limitation, but it is better understood as a deliberate design tradeoff that follows directly from separation of concerns and the end to end principle covered earlier. Keeping the network layer simple, with no per-packet acknowledgment and no state to track for individual flows, is exactly what lets routers forward enormous volumes of traffic quickly and lets the network scale to carry traffic for billions of devices without every router remembering the status of every packet passing through it. Whatever reliability an application actually needs is pushed up to the endpoints, where TCP or the application itself can add it, rather than being paid for by every packet on the network regardless of whether that particular application needed it.

A live video call is a clean worked example of why best effort delivery is often the right choice rather than a flaw. Voice and video are frequently carried over UDP using RTP. If a packet carrying a fraction of a second of video is dropped somewhere in the network, best effort delivery means it is simply gone, with no automatic retransmission. This is actually desirable: by the time a retransmitted copy of that lost packet could arrive, several more recent frames would already be due for display, so the stale, late data would be useless anyway. The application instead conceals the gap, perhaps by holding the last frame briefly or interpolating audio, and keeps moving forward with fresher data, which only works because the underlying transport did not waste time or bandwidth trying to guarantee delivery of something now obsolete.

Contrast this with downloading a software update, where every single byte matters and a silently dropped byte in the middle of an executable file could make it fail to run; that is precisely the scenario where an application needs to layer reliable delivery, built on a connection oriented protocol like TCP, on top of the network's best effort foundation rather than accepting best effort delivery on its own.
